extracted.intended_audience: legal academics, policymakers, practitioners, and law students interested in technology regulation and AI law
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly legal analysis of how existing doctrines and regulatory responses should apply to novel technologies (historical media, elevators, AI/LLMs), including when to adapt law versus create new rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral panic phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: New media or groups are often the subject of recurring “moral panics” in which perceived threats to societal values are exaggerated, amplified by media, and lead to calls for stricter control and regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the pattern (Stanley Cohen’s concept) and historical examples (novels, comic books, television, TikTok ‘bed rotting’) to avoid overreacting. Use the moral-panic lens to interrogate whether perceived harms are empirically grounded or amplified for rhetorical/political ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical suspicion of popular media as corrupting
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular, mass-produced lowbrow media have historically been condemned for bypassing critical faculties and corrupting morals (e.g., novels accused of promoting idleness and escapism; 1950s comic-book panic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proposed regulation, consider the long history of similar claims and whether they conflate popularity or accessibility with inherent harm. Cite historical analogies to temper regulatory zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware regulation that preserves incumbent power
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions are frequently rationalized as essential for public welfare but often mask motivations to preserve incumbent power and political structures against destabilizing information dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize stated regulatory purposes for hidden distributional or power-preserving incentives. Historical evidence (e.g., critiques of novels, gendered labor rules for elevator operators) can reveal such motivations and should weigh against overly restrictive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarifying existing law over creating new substantive categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically there is no need to change substantive law in response to new technologies; instead clarify how existing doctrines apply (e.g., conversion or assault remain wrongs regardless of the instrument used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before drafting new legal categories, assess whether established principles (tort, contract, property, free-speech doctrines) can accommodate the technology by analogy or clarification. Use examples (conversion, assault) to justify adaptation rather than invention of new rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of traditional tort principles to new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding tort doctrines—negligence, products liability, foreseeability, reasonable care—generally furnish the tools to assign responsibility for harms involving new devices (e.g., elevators, autonomous vehicles, medical devices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply core elements: duty of reasonable care, breach, causation, and damages. Consider manufacturers’ liability for defects, users’ liability for negligent use, and courts' assessment of reasonableness under the circumstances (with Restatement provisions cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation law governs LLM output by publication and fault, not authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation liability focuses on publication and the defendant’s mental state (typically at least negligence), not on human authorship; thus outputs of large language models can support defamation claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an LLM creator or distributor published a defamatory statement with the requisite fault. Use Restatement (Third) defamation standards and Volokh’s analysis as frameworks. Historical analogues (errant telephone book printing) illustrate liability without human authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to remove or correct known defamatory material
rubrics_metrics.description: A publisher who learns that its own statement is false and defamatory has a duty to remove or correct it; continued publication after knowledge can ground liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When platforms or model providers are notified of false defamatory outputs, failure to act can be treated analogously to continuing to publish one's own libels (see Volokh on distributing your own libels). Assess notice procedures and remediation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability where LLM output stems from defective product design
rubrics_metrics.description: If publication of defamatory content results from a defective design of an LLM (i.e., a design flaw), the LLM creator can be liable under products-liability principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze design-defect claims under Restatement (Third) of Products Liability: was there a safer, feasible design available at time of distribution? Consider evidence about training data, model architecture, and reasonable design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability despite absence of a superior design when publisher continues publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent a viable superior product design at the time of release, liability can arise if the model creator or publisher becomes aware of defamatory outputs and continues to make them available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish design-defect claims from continued-publication claims: the former looks to design choices at sale; the latter looks to post-sale knowledge and remedial steps (or lack thereof). Assess notice, corrective opportunities, and responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products-liability and negligence frameworks suffice for many AI harms
rubrics_metrics.description: When AI systems cause physical or economic harm (e.g., autonomous-vehicle accidents, faulty medical devices), traditional products-liability and negligence doctrine generally provide appropriate liability rules (manufacturers for defects; users for negligent use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Restatement (Third) products-liability categories (manufacturing defect, design defect, inadequate warnings) and negligence standards (duty, breach, causation, foreseeability). Courts and juries evaluate reasonableness under circumstances; map facts to these established frameworks first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and inscrutability problems require careful doctrinal development
rubrics_metrics.description: Some machine behaviors may defy easy attribution of fault to operator or manufacturer, particularly where no single design flaw is pinpointable; AI’s inscrutability poses challenges to fault-based compensation regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where fault is hard to attribute, develop doctrinal tools (causation doctrines, evidentiary rules, disclosure/forensic requirements, statutory adjustments) to allocate responsibility without wholesale creation of new liability categories. Consider policy tradeoffs in compensation versus innovation incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry custom is relevant but not dispositive to due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with industry custom is relevant to determining due diligence in construction/operation, but the usage of others is not the sole criterion and does not conclusively establish reasonable prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess custom as one factor among others; courts may find that an entire industry has 'unduly lagged' and that reasonable prudence requires adopting better available safety measures (T.J. Hooper principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly prescriptive, fragmented technical statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Early technology-specific laws often focused on granular mechanical details (e.g., rope tensile strength, brake mechanisms, operator qualifications) and produced cumbersome, rapidly outdated, and sometimes misguided requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor flexible, principle-based regulation over highly prescriptive technical rules to reduce ossification and obsolescence. Use historical examples (elevator statutes, sex- and hour-based operator restrictions) to show harms of narrow technical mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative process is prone to regulatory capture and ossification
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmaking can lock in soon-to-be-outdated technologies and be influenced by special interests, producing ossified requirements that hinder innovation and produce regulatory capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing statutory responses, build in adaptability (sunset clauses, review mechanisms, technology-neutral standards) and guard against capture by affected industries or incumbents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust can require demonstrable safety and clear standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological adoption often depends on convincing a wary public through credible safety mechanisms and demonstrations (e.g., Otis’s safety hoist demonstration that built confidence in elevators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate adoption by promoting verifiable safety standards, transparent testing, and public demonstration or certification. Regulators and industry can use such measures to reduce panic-driven regulation and encourage informed acceptance.
